title: Twitch API: Access, Tokens and Rate Limits (2026)
summary: Twitch API provides Helix (REST) and EventSub (real-time events), each with different purposes. Decide which suits your needs based on how each works.
body_markdown:
## Twitch API rate limits, quotas and EventSub limits


On every token, Helix, Twitch's REST API, meters a bucket of **800 points per minute** , so a failed refresh is rarely your first problem; spending the bucket carelessly is.


### Helix request bucket and headers


One point per ordinary call, and the bucket refills continuously. Every response carries` Ratelimit-Limit` ,` Ratelimit-Remaining` and` Ratelimit-Reset` .


Read` Ratelimit-Remaining` before you loop, because an empty bucket returns HTTP 429 and your retry logic then competes with itself. List endpoints cap a page at 100 items, so you follow the` cursor` value and each extra page costs another point.


For live detection, polling barely dents the budget.


The Twitch developer forum states that every 5 minutes is 2,880 a day and every 15 minutes is 960, so the choice between intervals reflects a trade-off between data freshness and API quota consumption. Rate limits aren't what rules polling out.


What rules it out is that you learn about a stream going live up to a full interval late.


If you would rather not hand-write the polling loop, describe the stream-live alert in Activepieces' built-in chat and it publishes the flow itself: a live flow in your account, the same artefact a builder would have assembled by hand, running under the same RBAC and audit logs as every other flow.


Each execution leaves a run trace, so a 429 from an empty bucket appears as a failed step with Twitch's response attached, not as silence. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


### EventSub subscription cost limits


When you move to push, EventSub has its own ceiling:` max_total_cost` . It's 10,000 for an app token and only 10 for a user token. Each subscription has a cost, and some types cost 0 or 1 depending on authorization.


A user-token integration can therefore hold **only a handful of subscriptions** before Twitch refuses the next one. A single WebSocket connection also tops out at 300 subscriptions, so a larger deployment needs several connections.


### Twitch EventSub polling, webhook and WebSocket transports


Look at the failure column first: the three transports differ most in what happens when your receiver is unavailable, not in speed. Pick based on that.


Transport Latency Subscription limits When the receiver is down


Polling Up to one full interval None beyond the request bucket Nothing is lost if you read current state; short-lived events between polls are missed


Webhooks Near real time` max_total_cost` 10,000 on an app token Twitch retries failed deliveries, then revokes the subscription if the endpoint keeps failing


WebSocket Near real time 300 per connection;` max_total_cost` 10 on a user token Events during a dropped connection are not replayed, so you must reconnect and reconcile


If you choose webhooks, you need a public HTTPS endpoint that answers quickly and verifies signatures. WebSockets need no public endpoint but need a process that stays connected.


**For anything where a missed event costs you something, add a periodic poll to reconcile whichever push transport you choose.**
